title: Incense, Ransom, Water, and Oil
summary: God finishes his instructions for the tabernacle's furnishings with a small gold altar for burning incense before the veil. He then orders a half-shekel ransom from every counted Israelite, a bronze basin where the priests must wash, a sacred anointing oil for the tent, its furniture, and the priests, and a holy incense that no one may copy for private use.
story: Moses is still on Mount Sinai, where he has been for forty days (24:18), receiving the pattern for the tabernacle, the portable tent where God will live among his people. Chapter 29 reached a high point with God's promise, “Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God” (29:45). Chapter 30 turns from the building and the priests' ordination to what will keep the sanctuary working day after day: incense every morning and evening, washing before every approach, a ransom paid for every life, and the oil that marks things and people as God's. Readers know what the characters don't yet: at the foot of the mountain the people are about to make a golden calf (chapter 32). The instructions for living near God are being written at the very moment Israel is preparing to betray him.
historical:
Like the rest of Exodus, these chapters are set at Sinai shortly after Israel left Egypt, an event dated either to about 1446 BC or to the thirteenth century BC (the Exodus introduction sets out the debate). Critical scholars assign the tabernacle chapters to the Priestly source, and many regard chapters 30 and 31 as a supplement, because the incense altar is missing from the description of the holy place in chapters 25 and 26, where the table and lampstand appear. Others answer that the placement is deliberate: chapter 25 describes the furniture of God's house, while chapter 30 gathers items that concern the priests' ongoing ministry within it.

Small horned altars of stone have been found at several Iron Age sites in Israel, including Megiddo and the sanctuary at Arad, where two stood at the entrance to the shrine's inner niche. The tabernacle's altar was wood covered with gold, but the shape was a familiar one. Solomon's temple had its own golden altar before the inner room (1 Kings 7:48), and the story of King Uzziah, struck with a skin disease for burning incense that only priests could offer (2 Chronicles 26:16-21), shows how seriously the rule of verse 9 was taken. The spices named here came from far away. Frankincense and myrrh are tree resins from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, carried north by caravan, and cinnamon and cassia most likely came from farther east, although the exact identity of several of these ingredients, onycha and the fragrant cane among them, is uncertain.
cultural:
Coins did not yet exist. Silver was weighed out, and the shekel was a weight, roughly 11 to 12 grams, so a half shekel was a small but real amount of silver. Counting the people was not neutral bookkeeping. A census was taken to muster men for war or tax them, and the age of twenty (verse 14) is the age of military service in Numbers 1:3. To count people was to claim them, and Israel's people belonged to God. The ransom confessed that. Later the census silver was melted into the silver bases that held up the tabernacle's frames (38:25-28), so the sanctuary literally stood on the redemption money of the whole people. The half-shekel payment later became a yearly temple tax, the tax Jesus is asked about in Matthew 17:24-27.

Incense filled the ancient world's temples and palaces. It honored a god or king, sweetened the air, and in Israel's worship it had another function: on the Day of Atonement its cloud covered the mercy seat so that the high priest would not die (Leviticus 16:13). Anointing with oil was how kings and priests were installed, and oil marked a person or object as set apart. That is why the recipe is protected and why copying it is punished. Being cut off from his people (verses 33 and 38) is a phrase whose meaning is debated: some take it as execution by the community, others as a punishment God himself carries out, such as early death or the loss of descendants, and others as exclusion from Israel.
literary: Exodus 25 to 31 is built as seven speeches of the LORD to Moses, each opened by the words “the LORD said to Moses”. The first, and longest, runs from 25:1 to 30:10; chapter 30 then holds four short speeches (verses 11, 17, 22, and 34), and chapter 31 has the last two, the seventh being about the Sabbath. Many readers see a deliberate echo of the seven days of creation: the God who made a world in seven movements now builds a small world for his dwelling. Within this chapter the order moves from the inner room outward and back again: an altar in front of the veil, silver for the service of the tent, a basin in the courtyard, oil for everything, and finally incense placed “in front of the Testimony”, as near the ark as anything in the chapter.

outline.t: The half-shekel ransom at the census

doctrines.note: Every counted man pays a ransom for his life, and the rich pay no more and the poor no less (verse 15). Before God every life needs redeeming at the same price. The incense altar itself receives atoning blood once a year, so even the place of prayer must be cleansed.

Holiness here is a quality God gives to objects and people by anointing, and it makes them his alone. The oil and incense may not be copied or used for private pleasure: what belongs to God is not to be absorbed into ordinary life, however pleasant.

Incense rising morning and evening before the veil became a picture of prayer in later Scripture, as in Psalm 141:2, “May my prayer be set before You like incense”. The chapter joins that daily offering to the tending of the lamps, making worship regular rather than occasional.

words.note: Kipper, to make atonement. The word appears four times in this chapter, for the incense altar (verse 10) and for the lives of the people (verses 15 and 16). Its exact sense is debated: some connect it with covering, others with wiping clean or with paying a ransom. In priestly texts it describes God's provision for removing what separates his people from him.

Kopher, ransom. The payment that buys back a life that would otherwise be forfeit, used in Exodus 21:30 for the price paid to spare a man whose ox has killed someone. Here the whole people are treated as lives owed to God and bought back by silver.

Mashach, to anoint. From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, which passed into English as Messiah; its Greek translation, christos, gives the title Christ. In this chapter the tent, its furniture, and the priests are anointed, and later kings will be too.

Qetoret, incense, the fragrant smoke burned before the LORD. The chapter uses it seven times, and the blend described in verses 34 to 38 is called most holy. Its use is tightly guarded: unauthorized incense on this altar is forbidden (verse 9), and the same word is used when Nadab and Abihu die offering incense with unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1).

christ: Several threads from this chapter run to Jesus. The ransom paid for each life anticipates Jesus' own description of his mission, “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and 1 Peter 1:18-19 says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ. The anointing oil stands behind the title Messiah, the Anointed One, and Jesus applies to himself Isaiah's words about being anointed by the Spirit (Luke 4:18). The incense of prayer reappears when Zechariah is serving at the altar of incense as the angel announces the birth of John the Baptist (Luke 1:8-11), and in Revelation, where incense rises with the prayers of the saints from the golden altar before the throne (Revelation 8:3-4). Hebrews says Christ always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25). These are patterns and fulfillments that the New Testament draws, not hidden meanings in the recipe.

hard.q: Why would counting the people bring a plague, and why the harsh penalty for copying perfume?
hard.a:
The plague of verse 12 has a later echo in 2 Samuel 24, where David's census is followed by a deadly epidemic. The Bible does not treat counting as evil in itself; Numbers is named for two censuses God commands. The danger lies in who owns what is counted. A census served war and taxation, and a ruler who counts his people is claiming them as his resources. Israel's people belong to God, who redeemed them from Egypt, and the ransom is the confession that their lives are his. Interpreters differ on how much of the older ancient Near Eastern fear of counting lies in the background, but the chapter's own logic is clear.

The penalty for copying the oil and incense (verses 33 and 38) strikes modern readers as out of all proportion to the offense. Its point is the sanctity of what marks God's presence. If the sacred oil could be poured on anyone and the holy incense burned in any home for pleasure, the signs that set apart God's dwelling and his priests would become ordinary luxuries. The debate about what being cut off means (see above) also affects how severe the penalty is. The chapter asks readers to take seriously that some things are not for private use because they belong to God.

questions: Rich and poor paid exactly the same ransom. What does that say about how God values each person, and where do you tend to measure people differently?
Incense was burned every morning and every evening. What would it look like for your own prayer to have that kind of regular rhythm?
The anointing oil could not be used for private pleasure. Are there good things given to you for God's purposes that you have quietly turned to your own use?
